newsitem.title: KENYA: YEAREND-Africa split between conflict and T-Bills.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Africa split between conflict and T-Bills.

text.p: Africa's split personality was unmasked in 1996 with parts of the continent girding up for more conflict and chaos while others discovered treasury bills and the Internet.
This geopolitical schizophrenia did not respect national frontiers. Low-intensity wars can coexist with a fledgling stock exchange in the same country.
Uganda, one of the World Bank's few African darlings, forged ahead with moves towards democracy and liberal economic policies bringing impressive growth.

Yet the army goes into 1997 fighting rebels in the north and west. President Yoweri Museveni was one of a handful of former African military leaders who won pluralist elections in 1996 but Uganda is at loggerheads with neighbours Sudan and Zaire, two wounded but dangerous giants.

The protracted civil wars in Sudan, Liberia, Burundi and Somalia simmered and the year witnessed the start of what many experts fear will be Africa's most far-reaching conflict since independence nearly 40 years ago.
In mid-October rebels in eastern Zaire, supported by Rwanda, launched a well-planned offensive.
Within two months they had seized the east and put the skids under President Mobutu Sese Seko, Zaire's strongman since 1965.
In passing, they dealt the biggest blow to French influence in Africa for many years. France was unable to persuade its Western allies to intervene and unwilling to do so alone.
MOBUTU WATCHES ZAIRE CHAOS FROM AFAR
Mobutu observed the action from Europe, where he underwent cancer surgery, and kept delaying his promised return.
"If Zaire should implode it will totally change the map of the region with consequences for the entire continent," said a senior official at the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
"(In 1996) We've seen one of the greatest crises, in Zaire and the Great Lakes region," said Richard Cornwell of the Africa Institute in Pretoria.
"That's going to be Africa's Palestine. It's a sore that's going to flare up nastily and fairly regularly," he said.
At the heart of Africa, bordering nine countries and with its land stuffed with strategic minerals, Zaire is worth fighting for.
The break-up of Africa's third-largest country is now on the agenda and few of its neighbours can be confident of escaping the fall-out.
"Post-Cold War Africa has become a less stable place, if anything," said Cornwell.
"Part of the reason for this is that the end of the Cold War has deprived the continent of any international significance it once had. Disputes and conflicts are seen as having no global meaning."
That was amply proven after eastern Zaire exploded. The outside world wrung its hands about the fate of hundreds of thousands of destitute refugees but did little.

The OAU is trying to fill the vacuum but its 53 members lack the cash and the will to cope with the rash of conflicts. Nelson Mandela's South Africa, the strongest economic and military power south of the Sahara, is refusing to jeopardise its own future by relieving Western powers of the burden of Africa.
AFRICAN BORDERS ISSUE IS NO LONGER TABOO
The OAU is chained to its post-independence charter, enshrining the arbitrary frontiers inherited from colonisers.

The taboo on even discussing a reform of the charter is unlikely to survive for long, many African experts believe. The single-minded government in Rwanda wants a "Berlin Two" to decide the future shape of Africa, more than a century after European powers met in the German capital to carve up the continent.
"The border issue is already being talked about in corridors," the senior OAU official said.
"Like it or not, it is an idea whose time has come."
Africa's southern cone is a relative haven of calm but in East, West and Central Africa there are few countries making genuine economic and political progress.
Most foreign donors reckon a leader of that sub-group is Ghana, where President Jerry Rawlings was comfortably re-elected in December.
Can countries like Ghana become a positive vanguard or will they be dragged down by the nations in chaos?
"...the two groups are slowly coming to some sort of distinction, but the chaos and conflicts will draw back the progress of the first group," warned John Makumbe of Harare's University of Zimbabwe.
MINING KEEPS GOING DESPITE AFRICA'S WARS
Although African conflicts are protracted, the end of the Cold War means that they are low-level and bereft of sophisticated weaponry.
This means business can go on, particularly in mining.
Liberia's rebels have financed their seven-year war with diamonds and iron ore. Angola's warring factions have kept going for 20 years with oil or precious metals.
The same scenario is unfolding in Zaire where regions like Shaba and Kasai are potential eldorados for miners of gold, diamonds and strategic minerals.
The rebels in the east have already told mining corporations that their investments and expansion plans are in safe hands.

"Irrespective of what happens in Zaire, Shaba is going to be developed. It is going to go through, the political shenanigans will have no effect," Johannesburg-based investment analyst John Clemmow said.
"Overall, I am very positive that we are going to see a significant recovery in the Zairean mining industry," he said.
But big investors operating in almost stateless environments want control of their own security.
"What we are likely to witness is that companies will go in with their own private armies, and it will be a return to the days of the chartered companies," said Cornwell.
